### Treatise on a Sober Life, anger, grief and lawsuits, 1558 (Luigi Cornaro primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Luigi Cornaro primary sources: Treatise on a Sober Life, anger, grief and lawsuits, 1558"]
Principle: Choose to let reason govern anger, and treat setbacks as tests rather than verdicts.
- Situation: Cornaro says he had a hot temper and describes being pulled into expensive lawsuits by powerful men, which so distressed his brother and other relatives that he believes it shortened their lives.
- What he did: he chose to see the lawsuits as a trial of his strength, kept his spirits up, and won a favorable decision. Elsewhere he says he resolved to make his choleric disposition give way to reason.
- Lesson: he treated temper and worry as things you can work on deliberately, and framing a hardship as a test kept him steady.
- Caution: attributing relatives' deaths to grief is his 16th century reading. It should not be used to blame anyone's illness on their feelings.

### Treatise on a Sober Life, the collapse and the turn, 1558 (Luigi Cornaro primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Luigi Cornaro primary sources: Treatise on a Sober Life, the collapse and the turn, 1558"]
Principle: When habits are visibly failing you, a change that lasts beats a plan you abandon.
- Situation: by his own account, Cornaro reached his mid to late thirties in bad health from years of overindulgence, with stomach pain, gout symptoms, fever and constant thirst. Treat this as his self-report.
- What he did: his physicians told him a plain, regular life was the only path left. He admits he had heard this before and ignored it, and had hidden his drinking from them. When he finally committed, he says he stayed with it and felt better within days.
- Lesson: the turning point was not new information but a decision to stop fighting advice he already had. Change begins when evidence and discomfort finally outweigh comfort.
- Caution: this is a man reporting on himself, and his stated ages are known to be inflated. Anyone with symptoms like his needs a doctor, not a 16th century memoir.

### An Earnest Exhortation, the claim of a peaceful old age, c. 1558 (Luigi Cornaro primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Luigi Cornaro primary sources: An Earnest Exhortation, the claim of a peaceful old age, c. 1558"]
Principle: Serve something larger than yourself, and hold health claims with humility.
- Situation: he writes, claiming to be in his ninety-fifth year, to persuade readers that a regular life leads to a cheerful old age. The edition's preface and text disagree about which of his late pieces came first.
- What he argued: many people ruin old age by carrying youthful habits into it, while a steadier life spares them the sickness, sorrow and fear of death he says haunt others. He also says he is certain of reaching a hundred.
- Lesson: he found joy in serving his city, particularly by advocating for the Venetian lagoon. Purpose steadied him.
- Caution: certainty about a long life is not a virtue and is not evidence. He also says grief passes him quickly; the guide should not present emotional numbness as wisdom.

### Treatise on a Sober Life, family pressure and a setback, 1558 (Luigi Cornaro primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Luigi Cornaro primary sources: Treatise on a Sober Life, family pressure and a setback, 1558"]
Principle: Loving people can pressure you off a working routine; change deliberately, not to please them.
- Situation: in his own late seventies, his family and physicians worried he was doing too little and urged a change. He gave in, he says, to keep the peace.
- What he did: he made a modest change to his routine, and within days reports feeling peevish and low, then a long fever. He credits his earlier steady habits for his recovery.
- Lesson: he tells this as a caution about dropping what works because others insist. The deeper point is that a change to a routine deserves a reason and a check on how you actually feel.
- Caution: he read his illness as proof of his method, which is unproven. Do not use his story to resist medical advice; it is one man's account.

### Letter to Barbaro, answering the skeptics, undated (Luigi Cornaro primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Luigi Cornaro primary sources: Letter to Barbaro, answering the skeptics, undated"]
Principle: Say the change was hard, and that the difficulty is part of the worth.
- Situation: a letter to Barbaro, Patriarch-elect of Aquileia, written when he claims to be ninety-one. Learned physicians visit him and conclude he must be specially blessed.
- What he did: he rejected that view, arguing his condition is open to any person. He admits the change was difficult for him too, and says he prayed for the strength to keep it.
- Lesson: he says people with a stronger constitution may live more freely than he does; his rules were shaped by his weakness. He also notes he cannot tolerate wine for two summer months, which weakens him each year. The point is that a routine has to fit one's own body.
- Caution: his talk of special grace and his boasting are self-serving. His own account of yearly weakness sits oddly with a story of perfect health.

### Treatise on a Sober Life, a full day in old age, 1558 (Luigi Cornaro primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Luigi Cornaro primary sources: Treatise on a Sober Life, a full day in old age, 1558"]
Principle: A life with useful work, friends and small pleasures does not feel like a decline.
- Situation: he describes his days at what he claims is age eighty-three, against the common view that life after seventy-five is death rather than life.
- What he did: he lists his pleasures, including conversation with friends, reading and writing to be of use, tending gardens, visiting his hillside lodge and villa, following the draining of marshland he had backed, and playing with his grandchildren.
- Lesson: his contentment came from purpose, company and beauty, not from a rule. He also says he wrote a comedy at that age, a claim we cannot verify.
- Caution: this is written to sell his method, and he was a wealthy landowner with leisure that most readers will not share.
